input: When a flow measurement is made, it is very important to have a clear understanding of the error that may be present in the reading, and this example uses a flow measurement in order to explain the difference between absolute error and relative error, as well as the way in which both of these differ from uncertainty. The absolute error is simply the size of the difference between the reading given by the instrument and the true value of the flow, and it is expressed in the same units as the measurement itself. Suppose, for example, that the reading is 175 units and that the tolerance on the instrument is 0.5% of the reading; the absolute error is then given by 0.5% of 175, which comes to 0.88 units. The relative error, by contrast, expresses that same error as a fraction of the reading, and in this case it is 0.5%. Uncertainty is a rather different idea, and it should not be confused with error, even though the two words are often used interchangeably in everyday speech. Whereas error belongs to one particular measurement and describes how far that reading lies from the true value, uncertainty describes the spread of values that could reasonably be associated with the measurement, and it characterises the doubt that remains about the result even when the measurement has been carried out with great care. To put the matter concretely, the absolute error of 0.88 units attached to a reading of 175 units is the very same error that the relative form describes, and stating the error as 0.88 units ties it to that particular reading and to no other.
target: Error in a flow measurement comes in two forms, absolute and relative, and a single worked case fixes both. Error is the difference between the reading an instrument gives and the true value of the flow. The absolute error states that difference in the units of the measurement itself. The relative error states the same difference as a fraction of the reading, most often as a percentage of the reading. A reading of 175 units from an instrument with a tolerance of 0.5% of reading carries the two forms together. The tolerance gives the relative error directly, 0.5% of the reading. The absolute error is 0.5% of 175 units, which is 0.88 units. One error, stated twice: as a percentage it travels from one reading to another of the same instrument, while as 0.88 units it belongs to the reading of 175 units and to no other. Uncertainty is a separate term and is not merged with error here. Error attaches to a single measurement and names its distance from the true value, a distance that cannot itself be measured once the reading is taken. Uncertainty attaches to the result as a statement of spread: the range of values that could reasonably be assigned to the flow, given the instrument and the conditions of the measurement. An error is a difference; an uncertainty is a dispersion, and the worked case's 0.88 units is an error, not an uncertainty. The distinction matters whenever readings are reported together, because a percentage can be carried from one reading of an instrument to the next, while an absolute figure stays behind with the reading it came from.
